diagnostic_evidence.quote: the intersection consists of exactly $\deg X=r$ points

issues.failure_explanation: At r = n_codim+1 the Bézout argument gives uniqueness whenever deg X = codim X + 1, not only for P^1 x P^{n-1} with O(1,1). Other Segre–Veronese varieties also have minimal degree: rational normal curves (one nonzero f_i, m_i=2), the Veronese surface (f_i=2, m_i=3), and O(a,1) on P^1 x P^{n-1}. Counterexample: S^4(R^2) with f=(2). Here n_col=3 and n_codim=1, so the formula gives r(f)=1. For r=2, however, a line meets the conic nu_2(P^1) in exactly 2 points, so r=2 is uniquely recoverable. The claim 'deg X > r for all other tuples' is false, and so is the stated formula.

failure_location.quote: For all other tuples $f$, we have $\deg X>r$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the special case by 'X has minimal degree (deg X = codim X + 1)'. List the Segre–Veronese varieties that qualify, using the del Pezzo–Bertini classification, and rerun the same Bézout argument for them.
issues.overall_effect: The 'largest r' formula underestimates r(f) for these tuples, so the r_max values derived from it are not sharp there.
issues.title: Case split for r(f) misses other minimal-degree Segre–Veronese varieties
issues.why_classification: The method survives, but the main formula must be restated using an additional classification argument; it is not just a local fix.

issues.failure_explanation: Inequality (eq: lojasiewicz) is stated for F_i, the restriction of F to block i with the other blocks frozen. It bounds |F_i(v^(i)) - F_i(v_*^(i))|. The proof replaces this by F(v_*) - F(v_(k,i)), the global gap, while keeping only the block-i Riemannian gradient on the right. That inequality is false in general: at a point where block i is already optimal but other blocks are not, the right side is zero and the left side is positive. The constants also depend on the frozen blocks, which change across iterations, so they need not be uniform. The Cauchy-sequence argument therefore has a gap.

failure_location.quote: Then equation \eqref{eq: lojasiewicz} holds for $\fv_{(k,i)}$ and together with \eqref{eq:function_increase}, we obtain

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use the Łojasiewicz inequality for F on the product of spheres. Bound the full Riemannian gradient at v_(k,1) by a constant times the sum of the block steps (Lipschitz continuity), then sum in the standard block-coordinate way (e.g., Uschmajew's HOPM proof).
issues.overall_effect: Global convergence of the iterates of PS-HOPM to a pSVT, and the algebraic rate, are not established as written.
issues.title: Block-wise Łojasiewicz inequality conflated with a global one
issues.why_classification: A replacement for the core convergence argument is needed, but it follows a standard framework and the stated result survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: If all block restrictions are convex over $\RR^{m_i}$
Global convergence of Algorithm~\ref{alg:psspm} then follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:power_method_convergence}.

issues.failure_explanation: The Hessian lower bound depends on the current value nu, and h is decreasing in nu. With F <= nu, gamma = c*h(nu) is smaller than the required c*h(F), so the stated direction cannot work. Even with F >= nu the bound holds only at the current point. Convexity over all of R^{m_i} needs it along the whole block sphere, where F_A can drop to 0 and the required shift is c*h(0) = c. The hypothesis of Theorem thm:power_method_convergence is therefore not met. The final step, which uses an undefined vector x and is 'same argument as' a cited lemma, is also not carried out.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Prove monotone ascent directly, adapting the subspace power method (SPM) argument for value-dependent shifts with F >= nu, and complete the Hessian bound. Otherwise fall back to the shifts of Theorem thm:power_method_convergence.
issues.overall_effect: The global-convergence guarantee with shifts smaller than one, which the paper uses to motivate faster convergence, is unsupported.
issues.title: Value-dependent shifts do not give the block convexity the convergence theorem requires
issues.why_classification: Needs a contained replacement argument; the fallback keeps convergence but loses the advertised smaller shifts.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: around every pSVT that is a second-order critical point of $F$ with positive singular value

issues.failure_explanation: A second-order critical point only has a negative semidefinite Riemannian Hessian. A null direction of H_{1,1} with H_{1,2} acting trivially on it gives J Psi the eigenvalue 1, so spectral radius < 1, and hence linear convergence, fails at degenerate critical points. The strict inequalities later in the proof also rely on definiteness. In addition, (eq: lambda mu) omits the factors ||v||^2 and ||w||^2, even though only ||v||^2 + ||w||^2 = 1 is assumed.

failure_location.quote: since $\mathbf{H}_{1,1}$ is negative definite, being a submatrix of the Hessian at a maximizer

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Assume a negative definite Riemannian Hessian (nondegenerate local maximizer), and redo the eigenvalue computation with the ||v||^2 and ||w||^2 factors; this yields lambda < 1. Then either verify nondegeneracy for the intended maximizers or state it as an assumption.
issues.overall_effect: The claim of local linear convergence around every second-order critical point is false for degenerate ones. The application to global maximizers of F_A additionally needs nondegeneracy, which is not shown.
issues.title: Local linear convergence assumes a negative definite Hessian, but the hypothesis is only second-order criticality
issues.why_classification: The added nondegeneracy hypothesis restricts the scope, and the intended application loses its guarantee unless further argument is supplied.

issues.failure_explanation: The sum over j != i has r-1 terms, so the correct estimate is |mu_i - <R_i,T_w>| <= (r-1) rho ||mu||_inf. This gives ||mu||_inf <= max|<R_i,T_w>| / (1-(r-1)rho), and only when (r-1) rho < 1. The bound with 1-rho does not follow. When (r-1) rho >= 1 the Gram matrix can be nearly singular, and then mu, and hence F_A, can be large relative to max|<R_i,T_w>|.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 1-rho by 1-(r-1)rho and add the hypothesis (r-1)rho < 1. Alternatively, bound ||mu|| through the smallest eigenvalue of the Gram matrix.
issues.overall_effect: The stated upper bound on F_A at critical points, with constant C, is not established.
issues.title: Coefficient bound drops the factor (r-1); the constant C is unsupported
issues.why_classification: The constant becomes materially worse and an extra hypothesis is needed, but a comparable statement survives.

issues.failure_explanation: The statement assumes only generic factors and dim A = r. If r equals the dimension of the ambient space, A is the whole space. Then every rank-one T' gives T' ⊗ R_(f) in A, so infinitely many rank-one left singular vectors have singular value one and uniqueness fails. The proof invokes r <= r(f) without it being assumed. It also misstates which rank-one elements lie in A: these are degree-d tensors, not the R_(f).

failure_location.quote: are the only rank-one elements in $\Acal$ (up to scale), since $r \leq r(f)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis r <= r(f). Then argue that a rank-one element of A has f-flattening a⊗b with a proportional to some a_k, so by independence of the a_i and b_i it is proportional to R_(d)^(k).
issues.overall_effect: The uniqueness claim is false without a rank bound.
issues.title: Matching theorem uses r <= r(f), which is not among its hypotheses
issues.why_classification: Adding a standard hypothesis, which the downstream uses already assume, restores the result.

issues.failure_explanation: For n=2 the corollary's own formulas give r(1,1) = min{4,k} and r(2,1) = 3. For k >= 4, (1,1) is strictly better (4 > 3), yet the stated threshold (n^2+3n-2)/(2n-2) = 4 assigns (2,1) at k = 4. The k=2 entry min{4,n} also disagrees with n_codim + 1 = n.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Treat n=2 separately: (1,1) is optimal for k >= 4 and the two tuples tie at k = 3. Also correct the k=2 entry to n.
issues.overall_effect: The stated optimal tuple is incorrect in the n=2 boundary regime.
issues.title: Optimal flattening for S^4(R^2)⊗R^k is wrong for k>=4
issues.why_classification: This is a local fix of a boundary case; the main n>2, k>2 threshold is unaffected.

issues.failure_explanation: Write K = C^{-1} - lambda a_u a_v^T. Then K C a_u = 0, but the left null vector is C^T a_v, since (C^T a_v)^T K = 0. The column space of the deflated matrix is therefore U (C^T a_v)^perp. Moreover, Ĉ^{-1} = O_v^T K O_u requires a_v^T C O_v = 0. With O_v spanning (C a_v)^perp, both conditions fail unless C^T a_v is parallel to C a_v. After one update, C = O_u^T C O_v is no longer symmetric, so (b) and (c) fail from the second deflation step of MSPM onward.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Take O_v to span (C^T a_v)^perp, both in the proposition and in the algorithm; the identities then follow by direct computation.
issues.overall_effect: Parts (b) and (c) are false for general nonsingular C. The deflation in Algorithm alg:psspm-deflation is incorrect after its first iteration.
issues.title: Deflation update uses C a_v instead of C^T a_v for nonsymmetric C
issues.why_classification: A one-line local correction restores all claims and the algorithm.
